subject: Civics
text: Which body framed the Constitution of India?
explanation: The Constitution of India was framed by the Constituent Assembly, set up in 1946, which completed its work on 26th November 1949.

subject: Civics
text: Who were the Interim and Permanent Presidents of the Constituent Assembly respectively?
options: Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha and Dr. Rajendra Prasad
Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru and Dr. Rajendra Prasad
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and Dr. Rajendra Prasad
explanation: Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha, the oldest member, was elected the interim (temporary) President; Dr. Rajendra Prasad was later elected the permanent President of the Constituent Assembly.

subject: Civics
text: Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee that helped draft the Constitution of India?
explanation: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly and is regarded as the chief architect of the Indian Constitution.

subject: Civics
text: On which dates was the Constitution of India adopted and brought into force?
options: Adopted 26th January 1950 and enforced the same day
explanation: The Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution on 26th November 1949 (celebrated as Constitution Day), and it came into force on 26th January 1950 (Republic Day).

subject: Civics
text: Why is 26th January an important date in the history of India?
options: It is the day the Constituent Assembly first met
It is the day India got independence from British rule
It is the day the Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution
It is Republic Day, the day the Constitution came into force, and it also marks the anniversary of the Poorna Swaraj pledge of 1930
explanation: The Indian National Congress pledged to observe 26th January 1930 as 'Poorna Swaraj Diwas'. The same date was later chosen to bring the Constitution into force in 1950, and it is celebrated as Republic Day.

subject: Civics
text: The Directive Principles of State Policy have been enshrined under which Part of the Indian Constitution?
explanation: The Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in Part IV (Articles 36-51) of the Constitution; they direct the State to work towards a welfare state.

subject: Civics
text: Fundamental Duties were added to the Indian Constitution, under Part IV-A, through which amendment?
explanation: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 inserted Article 51-A under a new Part IV-A, listing the Fundamental Duties of citizens.

subject: Civics
text: Which Fundamental Right protects a citizen's other Fundamental Rights in case of their violation?
explanation: The Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32) empowers a citizen to move the Supreme Court directly for enforcement of any Fundamental Right that has been violated; Dr. Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.

subject: Civics
text: Which statement correctly defines the 'Rule of Law'?
options: The Constitution is supreme over all laws, and all persons are equal before the law and courts
The executive may exercise arbitrary powers when necessary
Only laws considered fair by citizens need to be obeyed
Rule of Law means the absence of any written constitution
explanation: Rule of Law means that the Constitution is the supreme law of the land, no one is above the law, and all citizens are equal before the law and the courts.

subject: Civics
text: Which Fundamental Right grants minorities the right to preserve their language, script, and culture?
explanation: Articles 29 and 30, under Cultural and Educational Rights, allow any section of citizens to conserve their distinct language, script or culture, and permit minorities to establish and administer their own educational institutions.

subject: Civics
text: What is meant by 'Single Citizenship' under the Indian Constitution?
options: All Indians, irrespective of the state they belong to, are citizens of India alone, with no separate state citizenship
A person may hold citizenship of their state as well as of India
Citizens of neighbouring countries living in India automatically become Indian citizens
A person may choose citizenship of any one state of their choice
explanation: Unlike some federations, India provides for Single Citizenship: every Indian is a citizen of India as a whole, and there is no separate citizenship of the state they reside in. This promotes national unity.

subject: Civics
text: 'Begar', or forced labour without payment, is prohibited under which Fundamental Right?
explanation: Article 23, under the Right against Exploitation, prohibits traffic in human beings and begar (forced labour). Article 24, under the same Right, bans employment of children below 14 years in factories and mines.

subject: Civics
text: What is a 'Welfare State'?
options: A state that exists only to collect taxes from citizens
A state that works for the social and economic well-being of all its citizens
A state that is governed only by the military
A state in which the government does not interfere in the economy at all
explanation: A Welfare State is one in which the government takes responsibility for the social and economic welfare of its citizens, for example through the Directive Principles of State Policy.

subject: Civics
text: Which of the following is a Fundamental Duty of Indian citizens listed under Article 51-A?
options: To vote in every election held in the country
To pay income tax regularly without reminders
To compulsorily join the armed forces
To cherish and follow the noble ideals which inspired the national struggle for freedom
explanation: Article 51-A lists ten Fundamental Duties, including cherishing the ideals of the freedom struggle, upholding the sovereignty and integrity of India, and protecting the natural environment.

subject: Civics
text: How do Fundamental Rights differ from the Directive Principles of State Policy?
options: Directive Principles can be enforced by courts, while Fundamental Rights cannot
Neither Fundamental Rights nor Directive Principles can be enforced by any court
Both are equally enforceable by the courts
Fundamental Rights are justiciable and can be enforced by courts, while Directive Principles are not enforceable by any court
explanation: Fundamental Rights are justiciable, meaning a citizen can approach a court if they are violated. Directive Principles are only guidelines for the State in making laws and policies, and are not enforceable by any court.

subject: Civics
text: Assertion (A): The Directive Principles of State Policy are not enforceable by any court, yet it is the duty of the State to apply them while making laws. Reason (R): In case of a conflict between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, the Fundamental Rights would prevail. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are individually true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are individually true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both statements are true facts about the Constitution, but R (about resolving conflicts between Rights and Principles) does not explain why the Principles are non-justiciable yet obligatory for the State to apply.

subject: Civics
text: Who acts as the Chairman of the Election Commission of India?
explanation: The Election Commission of India is headed by the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC), who chairs the body responsible for conducting free and fair elections.

subject: Civics
text: Who appoints the Chief Election Commissioner of India?
explanation: The Chief Election Commissioner is appointed by the President of India and normally holds office for six years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier.

subject: Civics
text: How can the Chief Election Commissioner of India be removed from office?
options: Through a process of impeachment undertaken by both Houses of Parliament, as in the case of a Supreme Court judge
By an order of the Prime Minister of India
By a decision of the Chief Justice of India alone
He can resign at will but cannot be removed
explanation: The Chief Election Commissioner can be removed only through the same impeachment process used for a Supreme Court judge, which requires a special majority in both Houses of Parliament. This safeguards the independence of the Election Commission.

subject: Civics
text: Which pair of bodies have their members chosen through Direct Election?
options: The Rajya Sabha and the Vidhan Parishad
The Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha
The Vidhan Sabha and the Vidhan Parishad
The Lok Sabha and the Vidhan Sabha
explanation: Members of the Lok Sabha and of the State Vidhan Sabhas (Legislative Assemblies) are directly elected by the voters of their respective constituencies.

subject: Civics
text: What is the composition of the Electoral College that elects the President of India?
options: Elected members of both Houses of Parliament together with elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States and Union Territories
Only the elected members of the Lok Sabha
Only the elected members of the Rajya Sabha
All members of Parliament, including nominated members
explanation: The President of India is elected indirectly by an Electoral College consisting of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States and Union Territories (with legislatures); nominated members do not vote.

subject: Civics
text: The electorate (Electoral College) that elects the Vice-President of India consists of:
options: All members of both Houses of Parliament, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha
The Legislative Assemblies of the States only
The Legislative Councils of the States only
Members of the Rajya Sabha and the Vidhan Sabhas
explanation: Unlike the Presidential election, the election of the Vice-President is carried out solely by members of both Houses of Parliament; State legislators do not take part.

subject: Civics
text: Why is the President of India elected indirectly rather than directly by the people?
options: To keep the largely ceremonial office above day-to-day party politics and to maintain uniformity across the country, since a direct nationwide election would be impractical
Because the President has no real powers at all
Because direct election is forbidden by international law
Because the Constitution does not permit any direct elections
explanation: The President's office is mainly ceremonial. Indirect election through elected representatives of Parliament and the States keeps the office above party politics while still reflecting the will of the people, and avoids the practical difficulty of a nationwide direct poll for one post.

subject: Civics
text: The election held after every five years, to constitute a fresh House, is called a:
explanation: A General Election is held at the end of the normal five-year term of a legislature, to elect members to the entire House afresh.

subject: Civics
text: When a seat falls vacant during the term of a legislature (due to death, resignation, or disqualification of the member), the election held to fill only that seat is called a:
explanation: A By-election fills a single vacant seat that falls vacant between General Elections, without affecting the rest of the House.

subject: Civics
text: When a legislature is dissolved before completing its normal five-year term, and a fresh election is held to constitute an entirely new House, it is called a:
explanation: A Mid-term Election is held when a House is dissolved before its full term is over, for example after the government loses majority support.

subject: Civics
text: Which of the following is an advantage of a multi-party system of elections?
options: It offers voters electoral choice between candidates and encourages healthy competition between parties
It removes the need for elections altogether
It always guarantees a single party a huge majority
It prevents coalition governments from ever being formed
explanation: A multi-party system gives voters a real choice of candidates and ideologies and encourages competition between parties, though it may sometimes lead to coalition governments.

subject: Civics
text: Every citizen of India who has completed 18 years of age, irrespective of caste, creed, religion or economic status, has the right to vote. This principle is known as:
explanation: Universal Adult Franchise means every adult citizen of 18 years or above is entitled to vote, without discrimination on grounds of caste, religion, sex or property.

subject: Civics
text: What is a 'Gram Sabha'?
options: A general body meeting of all the adult members (voters) of a village
The elected executive body of a village
The judicial body of a village
An officer appointed by the state government to supervise a village
explanation: The Gram Sabha is a general assembly of all adult residents of a village who are registered voters; it elects and oversees the work of the Gram Panchayat.

subject: Civics
text: Gram Panchayat is the Executive Body of the village; the corresponding Judicial Body of the village is the:
explanation: While the Gram Panchayat is the elected executive wing that administers the village, the Nyaya Panchayat is the judicial wing that settles minor civil and criminal disputes.

subject: Civics
text: Why are lawyers not allowed to appear before a Nyaya Panchayat to plead anybody's case?
options: Because only government officers may speak before the Nyaya Panchayat
Because lawyers are not permitted to practise in rural India
So that disputes can be settled quickly and inexpensively, without the delays and costs of formal legal procedure
Because the Nyaya Panchayat does not recognise the existence of disputes
explanation: The Nyaya Panchayat is meant to provide quick and inexpensive justice for minor disputes at the village level; keeping out lawyers avoids the delay and expense of formal court procedure.

subject: Civics
text: In a petty criminal case brought before it, which of the following actions can a Nyaya Panchayat take?
options: It can impose a small fine (commonly up to about ₹100)
It can impose both a fine and a term of imprisonment
It can impose a fine of up to ₹1000
It can award a sentence of imprisonment for up to a month
explanation: A Nyaya Panchayat deals only with minor civil and criminal matters and can impose a small fine; it has no power to award imprisonment, unlike a regular court.

subject: Civics
text: What is meant by the 'Panchayat Samiti'?
options: The highest court for rural disputes
The judicial body of the village
The intermediate (block-level) tier of the Panchayati Raj system, linking the Gram Panchayats to the Zila Parishad
explanation: The Panchayat Samiti is the middle tier of the three-tier Panchayati Raj system, operating at the block level; in different states it is also known as the Block Samiti, Taluka Panchayat or Mandal Panchayat.

subject: Civics
text: Which is the local self-government body that functions at the district level in the Panchayati Raj system?
explanation: The Zila Parishad is the top (district-level) tier of the three-tier Panchayati Raj structure, coordinating the work of Panchayat Samitis in the district.

subject: Civics
text: Which committee recommended the three-tier structure of Panchayati Raj Institutions, and through which Amendment was this system formally added to the Constitution?
options: Balwant Rai Mehta Committee; 73rd Amendment Act
Ram Lal Anand Committee; 91st Amendment Act
explanation: The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended the three-tier Panchayati Raj structure of Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti and Zila Parishad; it was given constitutional status by the 73rd Amendment Act, 1992.

subject: Civics
text: Which Act guarantees 100 days of unskilled wage employment to every rural household that opts for it?
options: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA)
The Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana
explanation: MGNREGA (originally NREGA, 2005) guarantees at least 100 days of unskilled manual wage employment per year to rural households, and is implemented with the help of the Panchayat Samiti.

subject: Civics
text: In furtherance of its civic duties towards child welfare, the Panchayat Samiti has set up numerous centres in rural areas known as:
explanation: Anganwadis are rural child-care and nutrition centres set up under the supervisory/welfare functions of the Panchayat Samiti to improve the status of children.

subject: Civics
text: How can the head of a Gram Panchayat (the Sarpanch) be removed from office before completing the term?
options: He can never be removed before completing his term
Through a no-confidence motion passed by a required majority of the elected Panchayat members, or by order of the state government for proven misconduct
Only the Gram Sabha can remove him, with a simple show of hands
Only the Zila Parishad can remove him
explanation: A Gram Panchayat head can be removed through a no-confidence motion passed by the required majority of elected Panchayat members, or by the state government if found guilty of misconduct or misuse of office.

subject: Civics
text: A Municipal Committee is constituted in towns and cities having a population between:
explanation: A Municipal Committee (or Municipal Council/Board) is set up to administer towns with a population roughly between 20,000 and 3,00,000 (3 lakhs); larger cities get a Municipal Corporation.

subject: Civics
text: A Municipal Corporation is set up for large cities; which of the following is an example of a city administered by a Municipal Corporation?
options: A hamlet under a Gram Panchayat
A block headquarters town of 10,000 people
A village with a population of 2,000
explanation: Municipal Corporations are constituted for major cities with large populations, such as Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai, which need a bigger administrative set-up than a Municipal Committee.

subject: Civics
text: Which of the following is an obligatory (compulsory) function of a Municipal Committee or Corporation?
options: Providing safe drinking water and electricity for domestic and commercial use
Considering whether to levy new taxes
Constructing community halls and shopping centres
explanation: Supplying safe drinking water and essential civic amenities such as electricity, drainage, and sanitation are obligatory functions that a municipal body must perform; building community halls or libraries are discretionary functions it may choose to undertake.

subject: Civics
text: Setting up public libraries, museums, parks, and transport facilities for citizens is an example of which kind of function of the Municipal Corporation?
explanation: Discretionary functions are those a Municipal Corporation may choose to perform for the comfort and convenience of citizens, such as libraries, museums, parks and public transport, unlike obligatory functions which it must perform.

subject: Civics
text: The Nehru Rozgar Yojana is a scheme that provides:
options: Financial assistance to small artisans and the urban poor for self-employment
Free primary education to urban children
100 days of unskilled wage employment in rural areas
explanation: The Nehru Rozgar Yojana was an urban employment scheme offering financial assistance for self-employment to small artisans and the urban poor, implemented through Municipal bodies.

subject: History
text: Out of the following remains excavated at Harappan sites, which one best indicates the commercial and economic development of the civilisation?
explanation: Seals, often bearing pictographic script and animal motifs, were used to stamp and identify traded goods, and are considered strong evidence of the Harappans' organised trade and commerce.

subject: History
text: A dockyard belonging to the Harappan Civilisation has been excavated at:
explanation: A brick-built dockyard was excavated at Lothal (in present-day Gujarat), providing strong evidence of the Harappans' maritime and overseas trade.

subject: History
text: Potteries used in the Harappan Civilisation for preserving valuables differed from ordinary pottery mainly because they were:
explanation: Pottery meant for storing valuables was given a painted and glazed finish, distinguishing it from the plain, undecorated pottery used for everyday purposes.

subject: History
text: Consider these statements about the Harappan Civilisation: P: The Harappans practised advanced city planning with grid layouts. Q: They used a pictographic script that has not been fully deciphered. R: Evidence of large-scale iron production has been found at Harappan sites. S: They had a centralized governance system across sites. Which statements are correct?
explanation: The Harappans used a grid-pattern town plan (P) and an undeciphered pictographic script (Q). They were a Bronze Age civilisation with no evidence of large-scale iron use (R is wrong), and the absence of palaces or grand temples suggests there was no single centralised monarchy ruling all sites (S is wrong).

subject: History
text: Which of the following is valid evidence that the Harappans participated in a vast maritime trade?
options: The presence of Ashokan pillar inscriptions near the Indus river
The use of the Devanagari script on Harappan seals
The excavation of a dockyard at Lothal and the discovery of Harappan seals in Mesopotamia
The discovery of iron ploughshares at Harappan sites
explanation: The dockyard at Lothal and the discovery of Harappan seals in distant Mesopotamian sites are key evidence of organised overseas maritime trade carried on by the Harappans.

subject: History
text: Who are the traditional authors of the two great epics of India, the Ramayana and the Mahabharata?
explanation: The Ramayana is traditionally attributed to sage Valmiki, and the Mahabharata to sage Ved Vyasa; both epics, composed in the Later Vedic period, are important sources for Vedic society.

subject: History
text: What role did iron play in the economy of the Later Vedic Aryans?
options: Iron was used only for making ornaments worn by priests
Iron was considered sacred and could not be used for tools
Iron replaced cattle as the chief unit of currency
Iron tools, especially the iron ploughshare, helped clear forests and improve agriculture, boosting food production
explanation: The use of iron (called 'ayas' or 'shyama ayas') for tools and ploughshares allowed the Later Vedic Aryans to clear dense forests of the Gangetic plains and expand agriculture significantly.

subject: History
text: Which new crop assumed greater significance in the Later Vedic Age compared to the Early Vedic Age?
explanation: As the Aryans moved into the fertile Gangetic plains, rice cultivation, aided by iron tools, grew greatly in importance during the Later Vedic Age.

subject: History
text: What are the four stages (Ashramas) of a man's life mentioned in the Vedas?
options: Childhood, Youth, Middle Age, and Old Age
explanation: The Ashrama System divided a man's life into four stages: Brahmacharya (student life), Grihastha (householder), Vanaprastha (partial retirement), and Sanyasa (renunciation).

subject: History
text: A wealthy man in Vedic India who owned several cows (between roughly 1500 BC and 500 BC) was known as a:
explanation: In Vedic society, where cattle wealth was a chief measure of status, a wealthy owner of many cows was referred to as a 'Grihapati'.

subject: History
text: Which of the following is a recognised feature of Later Vedic society?
options: The use of units of value named 'Nishka' and 'Satamana'
Women were freely allowed higher education
Iron and bronze had not yet come into use
explanation: In the Later Vedic period, gold ornaments like the Nishka and Satamana were used as units of value in exchange. Unlike the Early Vedic period, women's freedoms (including access to education) declined, and polygamy became more common among the wealthy.

subject: History
text: How did the position of women change between the Early Vedic Age and the Later Vedic Age?
options: Women enjoyed greater freedom and near-equal status in the Early Vedic Age, but their status and freedom declined considerably in the Later Vedic Age
Women's status steadily improved from the Early to the Later Vedic Age
There was no difference between the two periods
Women had no role in either the Early or Later Vedic Age
explanation: In the Early Vedic Age, women could attend assemblies, receive education, and choose their husbands. By the Later Vedic Age, their freedoms were curtailed - child marriage increased, education was restricted, and they were increasingly excluded from public life.

subject: History
text: Who founded Jainism?
explanation: Jainism was propagated by Vardhamana Mahavira in the 6th century BC, as one of the major religious reform movements that arose against the rigidity of the contemporary Brahmanical order.

subject: History
text: Which of the following was NOT part of Mahavira's Triratnas (Three Jewels)?
explanation: The Jain Triratnas (Three Jewels) are Right Faith (Samyak Darshan), Right Knowledge (Samyak Gyan), and Right Conduct (Samyak Charitra). Right Speech is not one of the three.

subject: History
text: Raima is a follower of Jainism and is not attracted to material possessions because she believes in the principle of:
explanation: Aparigraha (non-attachment, non-possession) is one of the chief Jain vows, teaching followers to give up excessive material possessions and desires.

subject: History
text: Which of the following cannot be identified as one of the Four Noble Truths emphasised by the Buddha in his teachings?
options: The world is full of sorrow and suffering
One can overcome desires by following the Eight-Fold Path
The main cause of suffering is man's desire for sensual pleasures and earthly possessions
Suffering can be removed only through severe penance and self-mortification
explanation: The Buddha rejected extreme penance and self-mortification as a path to end suffering; instead, he taught that suffering could be overcome by following the Middle Path and the Eight-Fold Path, not through severe asceticism.

subject: History
text: Which of the following statements about the Tripitakas is correct: Assertion (Q): 'Sutta Pitaka' contains Buddhist teachings, sayings and ideas of karma and rebirth. Reason (R): The rules made for the Buddhist Sangha were written down in a book called 'Vinaya Pitaka'.
options: Both Q and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of Q
Both Q and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of Q
Q is true but R is false
Q is false but R is true
explanation: Both statements describe facts about two separate texts of the Tripitaka (the Sutta Pitaka and the Vinaya Pitaka), but R, which describes the Vinaya Pitaka, does not explain why the Sutta Pitaka contains teachings on karma and rebirth.

subject: History
text: Which is the chief literary source for reconstructing the teachings and history of Jainism?
explanation: The Kalpasutra, composed by Bhadrabahu, is the chief literary source for the life of Mahavira and the teachings of Jainism.

subject: History
text: Which event is generally considered the turning point of Emperor Ashoka's life, leading him to embrace Buddhism and non-violence?
options: The signing of the Treaty of Seleucus
explanation: The bloodshed and suffering Ashoka witnessed during the Kalinga War (261 BC) deeply moved him, leading him to embrace Buddhism and adopt a policy of non-violence (Dhamma) for the rest of his reign.

subject: History
text: Who was the Greek ambassador whose book 'Indica' is a valuable literary source for reconstructing the history of the Mauryan Empire?
explanation: Megasthenes, the Greek ambassador sent by Seleucus Nicator to the court of Chandragupta Maurya, wrote 'Indica', which describes Mauryan administration and the city of Patliputra in detail.

subject: History
text: Which book, a treatise on statecraft and the duties of a king, was written by Kautilya, the advisor of Chandragupta Maurya?
explanation: Kautilya (also known as Chanakya) wrote the Arthashastra, which deals extensively with statecraft, economics, and the duties and conduct expected of a king.

subject: History
text: Replace the underlined word to correct the statement: 'Yuktas served as the lawyers in the Mauryan Empire.'
explanation: 'Yuktas' were subordinate officials in the Mauryan administration who worked as tax collectors and accountants, not as lawyers.

subject: History
text: A district-level officer of today, similar to a District Magistrate, would be referred to in the Mauryan administration as a:
explanation: In the Mauryan administration, 'Rajukas' were officers in charge of the administration and justice of a district, comparable to a modern District Magistrate.

subject: History
text: What were the fundamental principles of Ashoka's 'Dhamma' as spread through his edicts?
options: Non-violence, tolerance of all religions, truthfulness, and respect for elders and for all living beings
Strict enforcement of Buddhism as the state religion by force
Abolition of taxes on all citizens
The supremacy of the Brahmin caste over all others
explanation: Ashoka's Dhamma, inscribed on pillars and rocks across his empire, emphasised non-violence, religious tolerance, truthfulness, respect for elders and ascetics, and kindness towards all living beings - not any one particular sectarian belief.

subject: History
text: Samudragupta is often called the 'Indian Napoleon'. Why?
options: Because he abolished the monarchy and introduced a republic
Because he introduced the French system of administration in India
Because, like Napoleon, he was an unconquered military conqueror who greatly expanded the Gupta empire through successful campaigns
Because he lost every battle he fought, like Napoleon's final defeat
explanation: Samudragupta greatly expanded the Gupta Empire through a long series of successful military campaigns and is said to have never been defeated, earning him comparison to Napoleon Bonaparte.

subject: History
text: Why was Samudragupta called 'Kaviraja' (king of poets)?
options: Because he was himself a skilled poet and a great patron of literature
Because he composed the Allahabad Pillar Inscription himself
Because he banned all forms of poetry in his court
Because he was born in a family of poets
explanation: Samudragupta was a gifted poet and musician as well as a warrior, and the title 'Kaviraja' (king among poets) reflects his own literary talent and patronage of the arts.

subject: History
text: Who composed the Allahabad Pillar Inscription, and in praise of which ruler was it written?
options: Megasthenes, in praise of Chandragupta Maurya
Kalidasa, in praise of Chandragupta II
explanation: The Allahabad Pillar Inscription was composed by Harisena, a court poet, and praises the military conquests and personal accomplishments of Samudragupta.

subject: History
text: Complete the given analogy: Ashoka : Piyadassi :: Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) : ________
explanation: Ashoka adopted the title 'Piyadassi' (pleasant to behold). Chandragupta II, who defeated the Shaka rulers, adopted the title 'Sakari' (destroyer of the Shakas), in addition to 'Vikramaditya'.

subject: History
text: Which Chinese Buddhist traveller visited India during the reign of Chandragupta II and wrote the account 'Fo-kwo-ki'?
explanation: Fa-hien, a Chinese Buddhist monk, visited India during Chandragupta II's reign and recorded his observations on administration and society in 'Fo-kwo-ki' ('Record of the Buddhist Kingdoms').

subject: History
text: Which famous astronomer-mathematician of the Gupta Age wrote the book 'Surya Siddhanta'?
explanation: Aryabhatta, the celebrated Gupta-era mathematician and astronomer, wrote the Surya Siddhanta as well as the Aryabhatiya, and is known for calculating the value of pi and explaining eclipses.

subject: History
text: During the Gupta administration, the village headman in charge of local administration was known as the:
explanation: In Gupta village administration, the headman of the village, responsible for local affairs, was called the 'Gramika'.

subject: History
text: Assertion (A): The Gupta period is known as the 'Golden Age of Ancient India'. Reasoning (R): Various Gupta kings established an efficient system of administration and brought about political unity. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is wrong
A is incorrect but R is correct
explanation: The efficient Gupta administration and the political unity it brought laid the foundation for the remarkable flourishing of art, literature, science, and culture that earned this period the title 'Golden Age of Ancient India' - so R correctly explains A.

subject: History
text: The Sangam Age in South India refers to the period when three Tamil kingdoms ruled the region. Which were these three kingdoms?
explanation: The Sangam Age (roughly 3rd century BC to 3rd century AD) is named after the three Tamil kingdoms that ruled South India - the Chola, Chera, and Pandya dynasties.

subject: History
text: The three Sangam assemblies held at Madurai are said to have lasted from which period?
options: Second century BC to first century BC
First century BC to third century AD
First century BC to sixth century AD
Third century BC to first century BC
explanation: According to tradition, the three Tamil Sangams (literary assemblies) held at Madurai spanned a long period from roughly the first century BC to the sixth century AD.

subject: History
text: Choose the correctly matched option for the following Sangam-era terms: A. Porul, B. Aram, C. Yavana, D. Inbam, matched with: i. Foreigner, ii. Kama (pleasure), iii. Dharma, iv. Artha (wealth).
explanation: In Tamil Sangam literature, Porul corresponds to Artha (wealth), Aram to Dharma (virtue), Yavana means a foreigner (usually a Greek or Roman trader), and Inbam corresponds to Kama (pleasure/love).

subject: History
text: Pepper, a highly prized export of South India during the Sangam Age that was eagerly sought after by the Romans, was referred to in Tamil as:
explanation: Pepper was called 'Yavanpriya' ('favourite of the Yavanas/foreigners') because it was so highly prized by Roman traders, who exchanged gold and wine for South Indian pepper, spices, pearls, and textiles.

subject: History
text: Identify the odd (mismatched) pair from the following: a) Aryabhatta - Surya Siddhanta, b) Malvikagnimitra - Kalidasa, c) Tirukkural - Tiruvalluvar, d) Fo-kwo-ki - Hiuen Tsang.
explanation: 'Fo-kwo-ki' was written by Fa-hien, not Hiuen Tsang (who wrote the travel account 'Si-Yu-Ki'), making this the mismatched pair.

subject: History
text: What was the position of women in Sangam Age society?
options: Women could not own any property under any circumstances
Women had no rights or freedom of any kind
Women were strictly forbidden from any form of education
Women enjoyed considerable freedom, received education, and some, like the poetess Avvaiyar, became celebrated Sangam poets
explanation: Sangam-age women enjoyed relatively greater freedom than in some later periods; several women, most famously the poetess Avvaiyar, were celebrated contributors to Sangam literature.

subject: History
text: The Brihadeswara Temple at Thanjavur was built by Rajaraja I and is dedicated to which deity?
explanation: Rajaraja I, a devout Shaivite, built the magnificent Brihadeswara Temple at Thanjavur, dedicated to Lord Shiva, one of the finest examples of Dravidian temple architecture.

subject: History
text: Which of the following statements does NOT apply to Rajaraja I?
options: He was not tolerant of other sects and religions
He built a few Vishnu temples as well
explanation: Despite being a devout worshipper of Shiva, Rajaraja I was known for his religious tolerance - he also supported the construction of temples to other deities and even Buddhist viharas, so the statement that he was intolerant is false.

subject: History
text: Which Chola ruler adopted the title 'Gangaikonda' (bearer of the Ganga), and why?
options: Rajendra I, after a victorious military expedition that reached the river Ganga in the north
Rajaraja I, because he was born on the banks of the Ganga
Rajendra I, because he built a canal from the Ganga to his new capital
Rajaraja I, after building the Brihadeswara temple
explanation: Rajendra I adopted the title 'Gangaikonda Chola' (bringer of the Ganga) to commemorate his victorious northern expedition that reached the river Ganga, and he founded a new capital, Gangaikondacholapuram, to mark the achievement.

subject: History
text: The map of the Chola Empire shows its wide-ranging conquests. Which of the following places was NOT conquered by the Cholas?
explanation: Rajendra I's naval expeditions extended Chola influence to Ceylon, the Maldives, and parts of the Srivijaya empire (Java and Sumatra), but the North West Frontier Province, in the far northwest of the subcontinent, was never part of the Chola Empire.

subject: History
text: The sanctum sanctorum of the Dasavatara Temple (built during the Gupta period) houses an image of:
explanation: The Dasavatara Temple at Deogarh, a fine example of Gupta-era temple architecture, is a Vishnu temple; 'Dasavatara' refers to the ten avatars of Vishnu depicted on its walls.

subject: History
text: The construction of the Qutub Minar in Delhi was started by one ruler and completed by another. Who were they?
options: Started by Shah Jahan, completed by Aurangzeb
Started by Iltutmish, completed by Qutub-ud-din Aibak
Started by Qutub-ud-din Aibak, completed by Iltutmish
Started by Alauddin Khalji, completed by Muhammad bin Tughlaq
explanation: Qutub-ud-din Aibak began the construction of the Qutub Minar, and it was completed by his successor and son-in-law, Iltutmish.

subject: History
text: The mosque built in Delhi by Qutub-ud-din Aibak is known as the:
explanation: The Quwat-ul-Islam Mosque, built by Qutub-ud-din Aibak in Delhi, is considered one of the earliest mosques built in India under the Delhi Sultanate; it stands near the Qutub Minar.

subject: History
text: Which Deccan kingdom, ruled by the Yadavas, was occupied by Alauddin Khalji?
explanation: Alauddin Khalji led successful campaigns into the Deccan, occupying the kingdom of the Yadavas of Devagiri, among other southern territories.

subject: History
text: Which of the following measures did Alauddin Khalji adopt to control the market during his reign?
options: He allowed merchants to fix prices freely with no state supervision
He banned all trade within his empire
He abolished all taxes on traders
He fixed prices of essential goods, maintained state granaries, and appointed a market controller (Shahna-i-Mandi) backed by spies to report prices
explanation: Alauddin Khalji's famous market-control reforms included fixing the prices of essential commodities, maintaining state granaries to prevent scarcity, appointing a Shahna-i-Mandi (market controller), and using spies to report on market prices and quality of goods.

subject: History
text: Why did Muhammad bin Tughlaq's scheme of 'Token Currency' fail?
options: Because the Sultan abolished the use of money altogether
Because gold was banned from being used as currency
Because the copper/brass coins could be easily forged, and people lost confidence in them, flooding the market with counterfeit coins
Because the coins were too heavy to carry
explanation: Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced token currency (copper/brass coins valued at par with silver), but since the coins were easy to forge and lacked proper safeguards, counterfeiters flooded the market, destroying public confidence and forcing the Sultan to withdraw the scheme.

subject: History
text: Why did Muhammad bin Tughlaq's scheme to increase taxation in the Doab region fail?
options: The scheme was never actually implemented
The tax increase was too small to make any difference
The region was suffering from famine at the time, and the harsh, unrealistic enforcement of higher taxes caused widespread misery and rebellion among peasants
The peasants of the Doab were too wealthy to be affected by the new taxes
explanation: Muhammad bin Tughlaq raised taxes sharply in the fertile Doab region at a time of famine; the harsh and insensitive enforcement of the policy led to peasant uprisings and further weakened the Sultanate.

subject: History
text: The First Battle of Panipat (1526), which marked the beginning of Mughal rule in India, was fought between Babur and which ruler?
options: Ibrahim Lodi, the last Lodi Sultan
explanation: In the First Battle of Panipat (1526), Babur defeated and killed Ibrahim Lodi, the last ruler of the Lodi dynasty, thereby ending the Delhi Sultanate and founding the Mughal Empire.

subject: History
text: Which of the following features was part of the new 'Imperial System' (Mansabdari system) introduced by Akbar for his army?
options: Only foreigners were allowed to serve as soldiers
The army was entirely abolished in favour of a police force
Officials and nobles were assigned ranks (mansabs) that determined the number of troops and cavalry they had to maintain for the emperor
Soldiers were allowed to choose which battles to fight in
explanation: Under Akbar's Mansabdari system, nobles and officers were given ranks (mansabs) that fixed their salary and the number of troops and horses they were obliged to maintain for the emperor, creating a disciplined, centrally-controlled army.

subject: History
text: Which policy of Aurangzeb made him unpopular among non-Muslims?
options: He promoted a new syncretic religion, Din-i-Ilahi
He gave non-Muslims important positions at court
He re-imposed the jizya tax on non-Muslims and ordered the destruction of several temples
He abolished all taxes on non-Muslims
explanation: Aurangzeb reversed Akbar's policy of religious tolerance by re-imposing the jizya tax on non-Muslims and ordering the destruction of certain temples, which alienated a large section of his non-Muslim subjects.

subject: History
text: Which Sikh Guru was captured by Aurangzeb and executed in Delhi after refusing to convert to Islam?
explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Sikh Guru, was captured and given the choice of embracing Islam or facing death by Aurangzeb; he refused to convert and was executed in Delhi in 1675.

subject: History
text: Who was the tenth and last Guru of the Sikhs?
explanation: Guru Gobind Singh was the tenth Sikh Guru; he founded the Khalsa and declared the Guru Granth Sahib the eternal Guru after himself, ending the line of personal Gurus.

subject: History
text: The Jama Masjid of Delhi, built by Shah Jahan, was constructed under the superintendence of:
explanation: Shah Jahan built the Jama Masjid in Delhi under the supervision of his Prime Minister, Sadullah Khan.

subject: History
text: 'Bijak' is a compilation of the teachings and verses of which Bhakti saint?
explanation: The 'Bijak' is a well-known collection of the dohas (couplets) and teachings of the Bhakti saint Kabir, who preached against idol worship, ritualism and caste distinctions while promoting Hindu-Muslim unity.

subject: History
text: Which Rajput princess, a devout follower of Lord Krishna, composed devotional songs that are still sung today?
explanation: Mirabai, a Rajput princess, was a deeply devoted follower of Lord Krishna and composed many devotional (bhakti) songs that remain popular across India.

subject: History
text: Who is the founder of the Chishti order of Sufism, whose tomb is enshrined at the Ajmer Sharief Dargah?
explanation: Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti founded the Chishti order of Sufism in India; his tomb at the Ajmer Sharief Dargah is one of the most revered Sufi shrines, visited by people of all faiths.

subject: History
text: Which Sikh Guru announced the end of personal Guruship and declared the Adi Granth as the eternal 'Guru Granth Sahib'?
explanation: Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, declared before his death that there would be no further human Guru and that the Adi Granth, henceforth called the Guru Granth Sahib, would be the eternal Guru of the Sikhs.

subject: History
text: The mortal remains of St. Francis Xavier, a Jesuit missionary who worked for the spread of Christianity in India, are preserved at:
options: The Basilica of Bom Jesus, Goa
explanation: St. Francis Xavier, who worked extensively in Goa, is buried at the Basilica of Bom Jesus, Goa; his body is traditionally said to be well preserved and is displayed to the public periodically.

subject: History
text: The term 'Renaissance' is derived from which Latin term?
explanation: 'Renaissance' is derived from the Latin verb 'Renascere', meaning 'to be reborn', reflecting the revival of interest in classical learning, art, and culture in 14th-16th century Europe.

subject: History
text: The printing press, which played a major role in spreading Renaissance ideas, was invented by Johannes Gutenberg in Germany; who set up this invention for the first time in England, in 1476?
explanation: William Caxton set up the first printing press in England in 1476, allowing the rapid spread of printed books and Renaissance ideas throughout the country.

subject: History
text: The cultural movement called 'Humanism' began to gain momentum in Italy during which century?
explanation: Humanism, which emphasised human potential and achievement, began in Italy in the 14th century and was a key intellectual force behind the Renaissance.

subject: History
text: The first important breakthrough during the Renaissance, in the knowledge of modern science, was made in which field?
options: Chemistry, through the discovery of the periodic table
Medicine, through the discovery of antibiotics
Biology, through the theory of evolution
explanation: Nicolaus Copernicus's heliocentric theory - that the earth revolves around the sun, rather than the sun around the earth - was the first major breakthrough of modern science during the Renaissance, challenging the Church's long-held geocentric view.

subject: History
text: The curiosity and spirit of enquiry unleashed by the Renaissance encouraged geographical explorations. Which Portuguese sailor discovered a new sea route to India?
explanation: The Portuguese sailor Vasco da Gama discovered the sea route to India around the Cape of Good Hope in 1498, inspired by the Renaissance spirit of exploration and the search for new trade routes.

subject: History
text: Who was the heretic who publicly burnt the Papal Bull of Excommunication at Wittenberg on 10th December 1520?
explanation: Martin Luther, the German monk who had challenged Church practices with his Ninety-Five Theses, publicly burnt the Pope's Bull of Excommunication at Wittenberg on 10th December 1520, a major act of defiance that sparked the Protestant Reformation.

subject: History
text: Pope Leo X sent which agent to Wittenberg to collect money, through the sale of indulgences, for building St. Peter's Basilica?
explanation: John Tetzel was sent by Pope Leo X to sell indulgences at Wittenberg to raise funds for St. Peter's Basilica; his aggressive methods provoked Martin Luther's protest and the start of the Reformation.

subject: History
text: Which books were written by the Renaissance humanists Erasmus and Thomas More respectively, both of which criticised the corruption of the Church and society?
options: 'In Praise of Folly' by Erasmus and 'Utopia' by Thomas More
'The Prince' by Erasmus and 'Utopia' by Thomas More
'In Praise of Folly' by Thomas More and 'The Prince' by Erasmus
'Utopia' by Erasmus and 'In Praise of Folly' by Thomas More
explanation: Erasmus wrote 'In Praise of Folly', a satire criticising clerical corruption, while Thomas More wrote 'Utopia', imagining an ideal, more just society; both works reflected Renaissance humanist criticism of contemporary institutions.

subject: History
text: What is meant by the term 'excommunication', as used by the Catholic Church against Martin Luther?
options: Formal expulsion from the Church and denial of its sacraments and rites
A ceremonial crowning as a Church leader
An invitation to join the priesthood
A formal pardon for past sins
explanation: Excommunication is the formal expulsion of a person from the Church, denying them its sacraments and religious rites; Martin Luther was excommunicated by Pope Leo X for his persistent criticism of Church practices.

subject: History
text: Which of the following can NOT be considered a Capitalist principle?
explanation: 'Social Cohesion' - the idea of social welfare and solidarity over individual profit - is a Socialist, not a Capitalist, principle; Capitalism emphasises profit maximisation, a free market economy, and competition.

subject: History
text: Complete the given analogy: Capitalism : Profit Maximisation :: Socialism : ?
explanation: While Capitalism is driven by profit maximisation for individuals or firms, Socialism emphasises social cohesion - the equitable sharing of resources for the collective welfare of society.

subject: History
text: Identify the odd one out from the following objectives of Socialism:
options: To set up Fair Price Shops and sell goods irrespective of profit or loss
To make effective provisions for public assistance when required
To promote equal distribution of resources
To produce even those goods which are of no utility to society
explanation: Socialism aims to produce goods that are genuinely useful for the welfare of society, under a planned economy; producing goods 'of no utility to society' goes directly against this core socialist objective.

subject: History
text: Which of the following statements regarding the Industrial Revolution is correct?
options: The Socialists were anxious to make large profits, keeping in mind only the welfare of the rich
It led to the development of the factory system
The agitation of the working class led to the rise of a Capitalist movement
explanation: The Industrial Revolution, which began in England, led to the rise of the factory system of production; it was the hardships suffered by workers under this system that led to agitation and the rise of the Socialist movement, not a capitalist one.

subject: Civics
text:
To enforce the Fundamental Rights, which of the following courts have the authority to issue writs?
1. Supreme Court
2. High Courts
3. District Courts
explanation: The Supreme Court (Article 32) and the High Courts (Article 226) can issue writs such as habeas corpus and mandamus; district courts cannot.

subject: History
text:
Assertion (A): The Early Vedic society was primarily pastoral in nature.
Reason (R): The Rigveda mentions cattle as a measure of wealth.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
explanation: Both are true, and the importance of cattle as the chief form of wealth (a rich man was gomat) shows that the Early Vedic Aryans were mainly a pastoral people.

subject: Civics
text: Which of the following is a provision of the Right against Exploitation?
options: Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour
Protection of the interests of minorities
Freedom from paying taxes for the promotion of any religion
explanation: The Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24) bans human trafficking, begar (forced labour) and the employment of children below 14 in hazardous work.

subject: History
text: If a person strictly followed the five great vows of Jainism, which of the following actions would they avoid?
options: Living a simple life without a desire to hoard
explanation: Satya (truthfulness) is one of the five vows, along with ahimsa, asteya, aparigraha and brahmacharya, so lying for profit would be avoided.

subject: History
text: A boy born into a Kshatriya family in the Later Vedic period was most likely expected to:
options: Become a warrior or ruler and protect the people
Perform sacrifices and teach the Vedas
explanation: In the Later Vedic varna system, occupation became hereditary: Brahmins were priests and teachers, Kshatriyas warriors and rulers, Vaishyas traders and farmers, and Shudras served the others.

subject: History
text: The early Buddhist scriptures (the Tripitakas) were written in:
explanation: Buddha preached in the language of the common people, and his teachings were compiled in Pali, which made them easy for ordinary people to understand.

subject: Civics
text: A person belonging to a tribal community is dismissed from government service without any reason. Which Fundamental Right is violated?
explanation: The Right to Equality guarantees equality before law and equality of opportunity in public employment, and prohibits discrimination on grounds such as caste or tribe.

subject: Civics
text: According to the Constitution, the number of members of a State Legislative Assembly shall be:
options: Not more than 500 and not less than 55
Not more than 500 and not less than 50
Not more than 500 and not less than 65
Not more than 500 and not less than 60
explanation: Article 170 fixes the strength of a Vidhan Sabha at not more than 500 and not less than 60 members (a few small states, such as Goa and Sikkim, are exceptions by law).

subject: History
text:
Which of the following statements state the main principles of Sufism?
P: True contentment lies in detachment from worldly desires and material possessions.
Q: Strict performance of religious rituals is the only path to salvation.
R: Love of God is expressed through love and compassion for all humanity.
S: Knowledge of God can be attained only through formal religious learning and scholarship.
explanation: Sufis stressed renunciation of worldly desires and love of God expressed through service of all people, and rejected rigid ritualism and mere book learning.

subject: History
text: The Chola kingdom was divided into provinces known as:
explanation: The empire was divided into mandalams (provinces), which were divided into valanadus or kottams, then nadus (districts), and finally villages (kurrams or urs).

subject: History
text:
Assertion (A): Muhammad bin Tughlaq advanced loans to farmers to promote agriculture after a severe famine in the Doab region.
Reason (R): The scheme succeeded because the loans were distributed fairly and recovered effectively, leading to increased agricultural production.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
explanation: A is true: the Sultan gave loans (takavi) to cultivators. R is false: much of the money was misused by officials and farmers, could not be recovered, and the scheme failed.

subject: History
text:
Assertion (A): Copernicus is renowned for starting a scientific revolution that redefined the foundations of modern astronomy.
Reason (R): Copernicus proposed that the Earth was fixed and that the Sun, Moon, planets and stars revolved around it.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
explanation: A is true. R is false: R describes the old geocentric view; Copernicus proposed the heliocentric theory, that the Earth and other planets revolve around the Sun.

subject: Civics
text: Which of the following statements about Universal Adult Franchise is INCORRECT?
options: It gives all adult citizens the right to vote, regardless of social status, wealth or education
It lets every adult citizen take part in the electoral process
It is a cornerstone of democracy, promoting equality and participation
It guarantees a responsible and efficient government in a democracy
explanation: Universal Adult Franchise gives every citizen aged 18 or above the right to vote, but by itself it cannot guarantee that the government elected will be responsible or efficient.

subject: Civics
text:
From the following, who can elect members of a State Legislative Council?
W: Members of Parliament
X: Members of the Legislative Assembly
Y: Members of local bodies
Z: Members of a school Student Council
explanation: One-third of the Council is elected by MLAs and one-third by members of local bodies (municipalities, panchayats and zila parishads); graduates and teachers elect one-twelfth each, and the Governor nominates the rest.

subject: Civics
text: What is the term of office of the Chief Election Commissioner of India?
options: Six years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier
explanation: The CEC holds office for six years or until reaching 65 years of age, whichever comes first.

subject: History
text: The Indus Valley (Harappan) Civilisation belonged to the:
explanation: The Harappans used copper and bronze (an alloy of copper and tin) for tools and figures; iron was unknown to them.

subject: History
text: Which of the following was NOT a feature of the residential houses at Harappan sites?
options: Rooms built around an open courtyard
explanation: Harappan houses were built of burnt bricks on raised platforms, with rooms around a courtyard and private bathrooms linked to drains. A pillared hall is a public building found in the citadel of Mohenjo-daro.

subject: History
text: Which of the Jain vows means "non-stealing"?
explanation: Asteya is not stealing; satya is truthfulness, aparigraha is non-possession and brahmacharya is chastity.

subject: History
text: The capital of the Mauryan Empire was:
explanation: Pataliputra (near modern Patna) was the Mauryan capital, described in detail by Megasthenes.

subject: History
text: The Tirukkural is a collection of couplets organised into how many chapters?
explanation: The Tirukkural has 1330 couplets (kurals) arranged in 133 chapters of 10 couplets each.

subject: History
text: The language of Sangam literature was:
explanation: The Sangam works, compiled by assemblies of Tamil poets at Madurai, are the earliest Tamil literature.

subject: History
text: The Tirukkural was written by:
explanation: Tiruvalluvar composed the Tirukkural; Ilango Adigal wrote the epic Silappadikaram and Tolkappiyar the grammar Tolkappiyam.

subject: Civics
text: The term of office of the Vice-President of India is:
explanation: The Vice-President is elected by both Houses of Parliament for a term of five years and can be re-elected.

subject: History
text: The Angas are:
options: The sacred texts of Buddhism, containing the rules for monks
The four Vedas of the Aryans
The sacred texts of Jainism, containing the teachings of Mahavira
explanation: The twelve Angas form the most important part of the Jain canon and set out the teachings of Mahavira.

subject: History
text: The Arthashastra describes the rule of which king, and who succeeded him?
explanation: Kautilya (Chanakya), the minister of Chandragupta Maurya, wrote the Arthashastra; Chandragupta was succeeded by his son Bindusara, the father of Ashoka.

subject: History
text: The graves of the people of the Sangam Age in South India are called megaliths because:
options: They were built of burnt bricks
They were marked by large stones placed over or around the burial
They were cut into rocks as cave temples
explanation: The word megalith means "big stone"; these burial sites were encircled or covered by large stone slabs, and contain pottery, iron tools and weapons.

subject: History
text: The famous bronze sculpture found at Mohenjo-daro is the:
explanation: The small bronze Dancing Girl, made by the lost-wax method, shows the Harappans' skill in metal casting. The bearded priest is a steatite figure, and the Pashupati figure is on a seal.

subject: Civics
text: Which constitutional body is responsible for carrying out a special intensive revision of the voters' list in a district?
explanation: The Election Commission prepares and revises the electoral rolls and conducts elections to Parliament, state legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President.

subject: Civics
text: Citizens gathering peacefully at India Gate to protest against rising air pollution is an example of which Fundamental Right?
explanation: Article 19 gives citizens the freedom of speech and expression and the freedom to assemble peaceably and without arms.

subject: Civics
text: Which of the following statements about a Money Bill in a state with two Houses is correct?
options: The Legislative Council can reject a Money Bill
A Money Bill can be introduced in either House
The Legislative Council must return a Money Bill to the Legislative Assembly within fourteen days with its recommendations
The Legislative Assembly is bound to accept the Council's recommendations on a Money Bill
explanation: A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Vidhan Sabha. The Vidhan Parishad cannot reject it and must return it within 14 days; the Assembly may accept or reject its recommendations.

subject: History
text: Modern Chandigarh is famous for its grid-iron pattern of roads. Which ancient city was planned on similar lines?
explanation: Harappan cities such as Mohenjo-daro had straight streets cutting each other at right angles, dividing the city into rectangular blocks.

subject: History
text: The officers appointed by Ashoka to spread Dhamma among the people were the:
explanation: Ashoka appointed Dhamma Mahamatras to preach Dhamma, look after the welfare of people and ensure tolerance among all sects.

subject: History
text:
Arrange the following Gupta rulers in chronological order:
1. Chandragupta I
2. Chandragupta II
3. Samudragupta
4. Skandagupta
explanation: Chandragupta I founded the empire, followed by his son Samudragupta, then Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya); Skandagupta, grandson of Chandragupta II, ruled later.

subject: History
text: A student reading the Tirukkural would learn mainly about:
options: The position of women during the Sangam period
The battles fought by ancient Tamil kings
Moral values, good conduct and principles of righteous living
explanation: The Tirukkural is a book of ethics in three parts: Aram (virtue), Porul (wealth and polity) and Inbam (love).

subject: History
text: According to the practice of the Catholic Church in the late Middle Ages, the easiest way for a wealthy merchant to have his sins pardoned was to:
options: Join a monastery and spend his life in prayer
Go on a long pilgrimage to the Holy Land
Purchase a letter of indulgence issued by the Church
explanation: An indulgence was a letter issued by the Pope, sold for money, which claimed to reduce punishment for sins; its sale by agents like John Tetzel provoked Martin Luther.

subject: History
text: A Mughal official fixes the land revenue of a peasant on the basis of the average produce of his land over the past ten years. Which system is this?
explanation: Under Akbar, Raja Todar Mal introduced the Dahsala (ten-year) system, in which revenue was fixed at one-third of the average produce of the previous ten years.

subject: History
text: The Renaissance is best described as a period in European history that:
options: Was a cultural rebirth inspired by renewed interest in classical art, humanism and scientific inquiry
Saw the decline of towns and the growth of feudal estates
Was mainly a political movement led by monarchs to centralise power
Marked the end of the classical period and the rise of orthodox religion
explanation: Renaissance means rebirth: from the 14th century, starting in Italy, there was a revival of Greek and Roman learning, humanism and a spirit of enquiry.

subject: History
text: Which of the following is an epic poem (mahakavya) written by Kalidasa?
explanation: Raghuvamsa (and Kumarasambhava) are Kalidasa's epic poems; Abhijnanashakuntalam and Malavikagnimitra are plays, and Meghaduta is a lyric poem.

subject: History
text: Who was the author of the Akbarnama and the Ain-i-Akbari?
explanation: Abul Fazl, a learned courtier of Akbar, wrote the Akbarnama, whose third volume is the Ain-i-Akbari.

subject: Civics
text: Who nominates members to a State Legislative Council, and what limits its total strength?
options: The Speaker; it cannot exceed 60 members
The Chief Minister; it must equal half the strength of the Assembly
The President; it is fixed at 100 members
The Governor; it cannot exceed one-third of the strength of the Legislative Assembly (and cannot be less than 40)
explanation: The Governor nominates one-sixth of the members from people with special knowledge of literature, science, art, co-operation and social service. The Council's strength must not exceed one-third of the Assembly's membership and must be at least 40.

subject: History
text: The famous educational institution of the Gupta age that attracted students from many countries was:
explanation: Nalanda, founded by Kumaragupta I in Bihar, was a great Buddhist centre of learning; students were admitted after a tough entrance test and studied free of cost.

subject: Civics
text: The elected head of a Municipal Corporation is the:
explanation: The Mayor is the elected head of a Municipal Corporation; the Municipal Commissioner is the appointed chief executive officer.
